title: A love letter to Jiu-Jitsu - Kengan Ashura's portrait of Grappling
summary: An essay contrasting Grappler Baki's sparse grappling with Kengan Ashura's precise, near-realistic portrayal of jiu-jitsu, using Imai Cosmo and others. NH explains why grappling matters in MMA, why strength matters even more for grappling than striking, and the stamina and long hours the art demands.
claims: No martial art has influenced modern fighting more than jiu-jitsu; being well-rounded is now unavoidable in MMA
Grappler Baki mostly ignores ground grappling and focuses on striking, while Kengan Ashura depicts jiu-jitsu step by step with near realism
Once someone takes your back and sinks a choke it's game over, which is why grappling must be learned
On your back you can't draw energy from the floor to strike; no martial art defends from the ground better than Brazilian jiu-jitsu
Rolling demands immense flexibility, strength and stamina
Widespread steroid use in grappling shows muscles matter; it is wrong to sum jiu-jitsu up as pure technique
Strength may matter more for grappling than striking, since pulling and controlling limbs benefits from resistance training more than punching does
Grappling and striking are separate endeavours and perfect complements
Heel hooks dominate no-gi MMA because they are devastating on opponents who can't defend them
With wrestling, judo and jiu-jitsu there are no lucky shots; mastery takes hundreds of hours of practice
